title: Branch Office vs Liaison Office Registration in Nepal
content:
Quick Answer

A foreign company that wants a physical presence in Nepal has two main routes: a branch office (can trade, contract and invoice) and a liaison office (non-trading, for research and coordination only). Both require prior approval from the Department of Industry (DOI) and registration with the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) under the Companies Act, 2063. The branch route is for companies doing business in Nepal; the liaison route is for companies only observing the market.

Choosing the wrong one is the most expensive mistake a foreign company makes here. A liaison office that starts invoicing can be shut down, and a branch office carries full tax and reporting obligations that a liaison office avoids. This guide explains the difference, who qualifies, the documents, and the process.

Which law governs a foreign company's presence in Nepal?

A foreign company establishing a place of business in Nepal must register with the OCR. Section 154 of the Companies Act, 2063 requires registration within one month of establishing a place of business. Two separate legal regimes apply depending on your activity:

  • Trading activity — register a branch office under Section 155 of the Companies Act, 2063.
  • Non-trading activity (market study, liaison, coordination) — register a liaison office under Section 156.

In both cases, approval from the Department of Industry (DOI) must be obtained first, and foreign exchange and repatriation matters are supervised by the Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB).

Branch office vs liaison office: the core difference

Feature Branch Office Liaison Office
Permitted activities Can trade, contract, invoice, import/export for the parent Market research, coordination, liaison only
Can earn income in Nepal Yes No (must be funded by the parent)
Tax registration (PAN/VAT) Yes Limited; not for trading income
Repatriation of profits Yes, after tax clearance and NRB compliance Not applicable
Renewal Periodic renewal required Periodic renewal required
Typical use case Executing contracts, projects, sales Feasibility study, market entry research

A branch office is an extension of the foreign parent and does not have a separately incorporated legal personality. That means the parent remains responsible for the branch's liabilities.

Who should choose a branch office?

A branch office suits a foreign company that already has business in Nepal — executing a contract, servicing clients, or running a project. If your Nepal operation needs to sign agreements in its own name, issue invoices, or move goods across the border, the branch is the appropriate vehicle. Because the branch is tax-registered, income earned in Nepal is taxed here, and profits can be repatriated after tax clearance and NRB approval.

Who should choose a liaison office?

A liaison office is for a foreign company that is not yet doing business in Nepal and only wants to study the market, gather information, or coordinate with partners. It may not earn income in Nepal, may not invoice, and is funded through remittances from the parent. It is a low-commitment way to establish a presence before committing to a branch or a locally incorporated subsidiary.

Eligibility and the negative list

Foreign companies in most sectors may apply for branch or liaison approval. However, Nepal maintains a negative list of activities reserved for Nepali citizens (for example, certain trading, travel and trekking, and cottage industries). Activity on the negative list cannot be approved for a branch or liaison office. Sector eligibility is assessed at the DOI approval stage.

Documents commonly required

While the exact checklist depends on the activity, applications typically require:

  • Application to the DOI with the proposed office details
  • Certificate of incorporation of the parent company (apostilled or consularised)
  • Memorandum and Articles of Association (or charter) of the parent
  • Board resolution authorising the Nepal office and nominating a representative
  • Audited financial statements of the parent for the last few years
  • Passport copy of the authorised representative
  • Power of Attorney in favour of a local representative
  • A commitment to fund the office (for liaison offices)
  • The underlying contract, licence, or project document (for branch offices)

Documents executed abroad generally need notarisation and apostille/consular legalisation, and non-English documents require certified translation.

The step-by-step process

  1. Prepare and legalise documents in the parent company's home country.
  2. File the application with the DOI, including the project or activity details and source of funds.
  3. Obtain DOI approval (permission to establish a branch or liaison office).
  4. Reserve the office name at the OCR.
  5. File registration with the OCR under the relevant section of the Companies Act within the statutory period.
  6. Tax registration — obtain a PAN (and VAT, where applicable) for a branch office.
  7. Open a bank account and complete NRB reporting for the initial remittance.
  8. Local ward/municipality registration and any sector-specific licence (for example, from the Nepal Tourism Board).

Cost and timeline

Approval and registration fees are modest by regional standards, but the realistic timeline depends on document readiness. Expect roughly two to six weeks for DOI approval and OCR registration once the file is complete, with foreign exchange and tax steps adding one to two weeks. Documents legalised abroad are usually the biggest source of delay.

Ongoing compliance

Both structures must renew their registration periodically and keep the OCR informed of changes to the registered office or representative. A branch office additionally has full tax filing obligations, must maintain proper accounts, and must route profits through tax clearance for repatriation. A liaison office must avoid anything that looks like trading — no invoices, no local income — and must document that it is funded by the parent.

Common mistakes

  • Registering a liaison office, then trading through it. This breaches the terms of approval and risks cancellation.
  • Missing the one-month registration window after establishing a place of business.
  • Skipping legalisation/apostille of foreign documents, which causes rejection.
  • Ignoring NRB reporting on the initial capital or funding remittance.
  • Assuming a branch is "a subsidiary." It is not — the parent carries the liability.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a foreign company have to register in Nepal? Registration with the OCR is required within one month of establishing a place of business in Nepal.

Can a liaison office earn income in Nepal? No. A liaison office is non-trading and must be funded by the parent company through remittances.

Can a branch office repatriate profits? Yes, after paying applicable taxes in Nepal and completing NRB compliance.

Does a branch office have a separate legal personality? No. A branch is an extension of the foreign parent, which remains liable for its obligations.

Is DOI approval needed before OCR registration? Yes. Foreign companies must obtain DOI approval before registering the branch or liaison office with the OCR.

Can a foreign company open a branch in a restricted sector? No. Activities on Nepal's negative list are reserved and cannot be approved for branch or liaison registration.

How long is the approval valid? Approvals are time-bound and must be renewed periodically; the renewal cycle is stated in the approval.

For your specific sector and activity, confirm eligibility and the current document checklist with the DOI and a Nepal-licensed practitioner before committing to a structure.

title: Business Visa in Nepal for Foreign Investors: How the Investor Visa Works
content:
Quick Answer

In Nepal, a business visa for a foreign investor is not a standalone product — it follows the investment. Once your investment is approved under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), 2075 (2019), the Department of Industry (DOI) or the Investment Board Nepal (IBN) recommends you to the Department of Immigration, which issues the business visa. The investor, authorised company representatives, and dependent family members can qualify. The visa must be renewed, usually annually, and it lapses if you abandon the investment or let it go dormant.

Which law governs the investor visa in Nepal?

The investor visa sits at the intersection of three regimes:

  • FITTA, 2075 (2019) — foreign investment approval, which is the foundation of the visa.
  • Immigration Act, 2049 (1992) and the Immigration Rules, 2054 — the visa categories and issuance procedure.
  • Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) rules — foreign exchange and repatriation compliance.

The practical point is that immigration follows investment approval. Without an approved investment, there is no basis for an investor business visa.

Who can get a business visa as an investor?

Broadly, the following can be recommended for a business visa:

  • A foreign investor who has made an approved investment in a Nepali company or industry.
  • Authorised representatives of a foreign corporate investor, where the investor is a company.
  • In certain cases, dependent family members (spouse and children), subject to immigration rules.

The visa is tied to the enterprise. If the investment is not maintained, the basis for the visa weakens.

The step-by-step process

  1. Obtain foreign investment approval from the DOI (or IBN for larger projects) under FITTA 2019.
  2. Incorporate or take shares in the Nepali company and have the capital brought in through banking channels, with NRB reporting.
  3. Apply to the DOI/IBN for a recommendation letter for the business visa, supported by evidence of the investment.
  4. Apply to the Department of Immigration with the recommendation and supporting documents.
  5. Receive and renew the business visa; renewals generally track the status of the investment.

Typical documents

  • FITTA approval and the foreign investment certificate
  • Company registration certificate and PAN of the Nepali enterprise
  • Evidence of capital inflow and NRB reporting
  • Recommendation letter from the DOI/IBN
  • Passport valid for the necessary period, and photograph(s)
  • Board resolution or appointment document for representatives
  • Proof of relationship for dependents (marriage/birth certificates, legalised)

Duration and renewal

Business visas for investors are granted for a defined period and are renewable, typically annually, provided the investment remains in good standing. Because the term and renewal conditions can change with policy and with the specifics of the approval, confirm the current duration with the DOI and Department of Immigration at the time of application.

Can you convert a tourist visa into a business visa?

Foreigners often enter Nepal on a tourist visa and then secure investment approval. Conversion is possible in accordance with immigration rules once there is an approved investment and a DOI/IBN recommendation, but it is not automatic. Overstaying while waiting for approvals attracts penalties, so the sequencing matters: secure the investment approval and recommendation first, and regularise status promptly.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming the visa comes first. The investment approval comes first; the visa follows.
  • Bringing capital in informally. Funds must enter through banking channels with NRB reporting, or the investment (and thus the visa basis) is defective.
  • Letting the company go dormant. A dormant or non-compliant investment undermines visa renewals.
  • Overstaying. Do not let a tourist visa expire while waiting for approvals.
  • Forgetting dependents' documentation. Relationship documents must be legalised and translated.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get a business visa without investing? No. The investor business visa is based on an approved investment under FITTA 2019. There is no investor visa independent of the investment.

Who issues the business visa? The Department of Immigration issues it, on the recommendation of the DOI or IBN.

Can my family come with me? Dependent family members may qualify, subject to immigration rules and proper documentation.

Does the visa last as long as my investment? Renewals generally track the investment's status, but the visa is issued for defined periods and must be renewed.

What happens if I repatriate my capital? The visa basis is the maintained investment; exiting the investment can affect your ability to renew.

Can I work in the company on this visa? The visa supports your role as an investor or authorised representative; other employment requires separate compliance with labour and immigration rules.

Visa durations, documentation and fees change with policy. Confirm the current requirements with the DOI/IBN and the Department of Immigration, and with a Nepal-licensed practitioner, before you travel.

title: Indian Investors Registering a Company in Nepal: 2026 Guide
content:
Quick Answer

Indian investors can register a company in Nepal on essentially the same footing as other foreign investors, under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), 2075 (2019) and the Companies Act, 2063. India is among Nepal's largest sources of foreign direct investment, and Nepali law generally permits up to 100% foreign ownership in sectors not on the negative list. The process runs through the Department of Industry (DOI) or Investment Board Nepal (IBN), the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR), and the Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). What differs for Indian investors is mostly practical: cross-border documentation, currency and banking treatment, and the India–Nepal tax treaty.

Is Indian investment treated differently?

Indian investors are foreign investors under FITTA 2019. The framework — minimum investment, sector eligibility, approval authority, and repatriation — applies the same way. In practice, Indian investors benefit from deep business links, a shared open border, and the India–Nepal Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), which can reduce withholding on certain payments. Because Indian rupees are convertible at the border in practice, funding arrangements can be simpler than for other investors, but NRB reporting and banking-channel requirements still apply.

Legal framework

  • Companies Act, 2063 (2006) — incorporation and governance.
  • FITTA, 2075 (2019) — foreign investment approval and repatriation.
  • Industrial Enterprises Act, 2076 (2020) — classification and incentives.
  • Nepal Rastra Bank rules — foreign exchange, capital inflow, and remittance.
  • India–Nepal DTAA — relief from double taxation on cross-border income.

Ownership and the negative list

Most sectors allow full foreign ownership, including by Indian companies. However, a negative list reserves certain activities for Nepali citizens — for example, parts of retail trading, cottage and small industries, travel and trekking agencies, and certain services. Sector eligibility is confirmed at the approval stage. Indian investors planning a joint venture should confirm early whether their activity permits 100% ownership or requires a Nepali partner.

Minimum investment

FITTA sets a general minimum foreign investment threshold per foreign investor, and the figure applies per investor — so in a joint venture each foreign shareholder must meet it. Because the threshold in Nepali rupees has been adjusted over time, confirm the current amount with the DOI or a licensed practitioner before you commit capital.

The step-by-step process

  1. Confirm sector eligibility against the negative list.
  2. Reserve the company name at the OCR.
  3. Apply for foreign investment approval to the DOI (or IBN above the applicable project-size threshold).
  4. Incorporate the company at the OCR — file the Memorandum and Articles of Association with the approved FDI details.
  5. Register for PAN and VAT at the Inland Revenue Department; register with the local ward.
  6. Open a bank account and bring the approved capital in through banking channels.
  7. Complete NRB reporting confirming the capital inflow (and any technology transfer).
  8. Obtain sector licences where required (for example, tourism or education).

Documents commonly required

  • Passport or corporate registration documents of the Indian investor
  • Certificate of incorporation and board resolution (for a corporate investor)
  • Memorandum and Articles of Association of the parent, where applicable
  • Source-of-funds declaration and project report
  • Proof of registered office address in Nepal (lease/ownership + owner's consent)
  • Director and shareholder consent letters
  • Notarised/apostilled and translated documents where executed in India

Tax and repatriation

A company incorporated in Nepal is a Nepali tax resident and is taxed on its income here. Dividends distributed to the Indian parent may attract withholding tax, which the India–Nepal DTAA can affect. Profits and dividends can be repatriated after tax clearance and NRB approval. An Indian investor should also consider the home-country tax treatment of the Nepali income and any foreign tax credit under the DTAA.

Timeline

Expect roughly two to six weeks for approval and incorporation once documents are ready, with tax, banking and NRB steps adding one to two weeks. Cross-border document legalisation and sector approvals are the usual sources of delay.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming Indian investors are exempt from FITTA approval. They are not.
  • Ignoring the negative list and planning a structure that cannot be approved.
  • Bringing funds informally. Capital must be documented through banking channels with NRB reporting.
  • Missing the per-investor minimum in a joint venture.
  • Overlooking the DTAA and paying unnecessary withholding.

Frequently asked questions

Can an Indian citizen own 100% of a Nepali company? In sectors not on the negative list, yes — up to 100% foreign ownership is generally permitted. Restricted sectors require different treatment.

Does Indian investment need DOI approval? Yes. Indian investors are foreign investors under FITTA 2019 and require approval.

Is the minimum investment lower for Indian investors? The general threshold applies to foreign investors; confirm the current figure, as it is set in Nepali rupees and can change.

Can an Indian company open a branch in Nepal instead? Yes. A foreign company (including an Indian one) may register a branch or liaison office, subject to DOI approval and OCR registration.

How long does it take? Typically two to six weeks for approval and incorporation once the file is complete.

Can profits be sent back to India? Yes, after tax clearance and NRB approval, and subject to the DTAA.

Minimum investment amounts, sector lists and tax rates change. Verify the current position with the DOI, NRB and a Nepal-licensed practitioner before investing.

title: Can Foreigners Own a Travel or Trekking Agency in Nepal?
content:
Quick Answer

Foreigners cannot fully own a travel or trekking agency in Nepal. Travel agencies, trekking agencies, rafting operators and similar tourism businesses are reserved for Nepali citizens under Nepal's tourism and investment rules. A foreign investor can, however, hold a minority share in a joint venture with Nepali partners where the law permits, and can own hotels and resorts 100%. This is one of the clearest "negative list" areas of Nepali investment law, so getting the structure right at the outset is essential.

Why can't foreigners own a trekking agency in Nepal?

Nepal's tourism licensing is built on the Tourism Act, 2035 (1978) and the regulations made under it, administered by the Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) and the Department of Tourism. Activities considered traditional, people-intensive tourism services — travel and trekking agencies, rafting, and certain guiding services — are reserved for Nepali citizens. The negative list under Nepal's investment framework mirrors this: these activities are not open to full foreign ownership.

The policy rationale is to protect livelihoods in sectors that are labour-intensive and culturally tied. As a result, a foreigner cannot simply register a trekking agency in their own name.

What can foreign investors own in tourism?

Tourism activity Foreign ownership
Hotels and resorts Up to 100%
Travel and trekking agencies Reserved for Nepali citizens (foreign minority possible in some cases)
Rafting and similar adventure operations Restricted
Airlines and aviation Sector-specific rules and caps

Hotels and resorts are the open door. A foreign investor can own and operate a hotel or resort outright, and can also invest in tourism infrastructure. For agencies, the workable route is a joint venture in which Nepali citizens hold the controlling stake required by law, with the foreign partner taking a permitted minority position.

Can a foreigner invest in a trekking agency through a joint venture?

In some configurations, yes — a foreign investor may hold a minority share in a trekking or travel agency alongside Nepali shareholders, provided the activity and the shareholding comply with the negative list and tourism licensing rules. Because the exact permitted ratios and activity definitions are set by policy that changes, the shareholding structure must be confirmed with the NTB/Department of Tourism and the Department of Industry before incorporation. A structure that gives the foreign investor effective control of a reserved activity is not approvable.

If the business is Nepali-owned, how is a travel/trekking agency registered?

For a Nepali-owned agency, the steps are:

  1. Register the company at the Office of the Company Registrar (and PAN/VAT at the IRD).
  2. Apply for the tourism licence from the Nepal Tourism Board / Department of Tourism, meeting the prescribed deposit/guarantee and office requirements.
  3. Complete local ward registration and any sector conditions (office, staff, insurance).
  4. Renew the licence periodically as required.

The licence — not just the company registration — is what authorises trading as a travel or trekking agency, and it is held in the name of the eligible (Nepali-controlled) entity.

What a foreign investor should consider instead

If your interest is tourism exposure in Nepal, the more reliable routes are:

  • Own a hotel or resort (up to 100% foreign ownership).
  • Enter a lawful joint venture in an agency with Nepali partners holding the required control, with a properly documented foreign minority stake.
  • Invest in tourism infrastructure — lodges, wellness, and hospitality projects — where foreign ownership is permitted.
  • Contract with licensed Nepali agencies for on-the-ground services rather than trying to own a reserved activity.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming "I can open a trekking agency like any company." Reserved activities are not open to full foreign ownership.
  • Structuring a minority stake that actually controls the agency. This is not approvable.
  • Getting the company registered but not the NTB licence. Company registration does not authorise agency trading.
  • Under-capitalising. Licensing has deposit and office requirements.

Frequently asked questions

Can a foreigner own a travel agency in Nepal? No — travel and trekking agencies are reserved for Nepali citizens. A permitted minority joint venture may be possible in some cases.

Can a foreigner own a hotel in Nepal? Yes. Hotels and resorts can be up to 100% foreign-owned.

Can I own a trekking agency as an NRN? The reserved-activity rules turn on citizenship and control of the activity; the position for non-resident Nepalis should be confirmed with the NTB and DOI for your specific case.

What licence does a trekking agency need? A licence from the Nepal Tourism Board / Department of Tourism, in addition to company registration and PAN/VAT.

Can I be a trekking guide as a foreigner? Guiding in reserved categories is generally restricted to Nepali citizens.

What is the safest tourism investment for a foreigner? Hotels and resorts, where full foreign ownership is permitted, or a properly structured joint venture.

Tourism licensing rules and permitted shareholding ratios change. Confirm the current position with the Nepal Tourism Board and the Department of Industry, and take Nepal-licensed advice, before committing to a structure.

The 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling's effect on specific project sites requires independent legal analysis. All project-specific determinations should be made with Nepal-registered energy law practitioners and confirmed with DOED, IBN, NEA, and NRB.

🎯 Direct Answer — How to Register Hydropower in Nepal

Hydropower registration in Nepal requires two licenses under the Electricity Act 1992: a Survey License (Adhyayan Anumati Patra) from DOED — valid up to 5 years — to study a river stretch, and a Generation License (Utpadan Anumati Patra) for 30–35 years to build and operate. Projects above 200 MW or NPR 6 billion go to IBN. Foreign investors also need FDI approval under FITTA 2019. A PPA with NEA is required before construction financing.

How to Use This GuideThis article describes Nepal's hydropower registration framework accurately. It cannot confirm whether your river stretch is available, what PPA tariff applies to your project, or whether your site is affected by the 2024 ruling. Those require direct DOED engagement or legal counsel.

Executive Summary

Nepal holds approximately 83,000 MW of theoretical hydropower potential. [7] Installed capacity reached approximately 3,200 MW by 2026, with private developers accounting for more than 80% of that base. [10] According to IPPAN's January 2026 report, domestic bank loans to hydropower exceeded NPR 447 billion — against a total national banking portfolio of NPR 5,563 billion. [10]

Registration follows a dual-stage process under the Electricity Act 1992: [1] a Survey License for site study, then a Generation License for construction and operation. Environmental clearance, water permits, forest land clearance, FDI approval, and a PPA with NEA run as parallel and partially overlapping processes under different agencies on different timelines. [4][5]

An empirical study of 34 private projects found virtually all missed their RCOD by 15–36 months, with forest clearance delays as the primary cause — not regulatory or construction failure. [12] Financial models built on statutory timelines rather than this empirical data do not survive first-year lender review.

I. The Three-Gate Approval Model: How Nepal's Hydropower Registration Actually Works Reference Level

Based on Pluto Associates's experience handling hydropower licensing applications since 2018, Nepal's hydropower registration is best understood as a Three-Gate Approval Model — three sequential eligibility tests that must each be passed before the next phase is meaningful. Developers who treat registration as a single linear process typically discover the three-gate structure only when they encounter the second or third gate unexpectedly late.

Gate 1 — Eligibility

Can You Apply at All?

  • Is the river stretch available in DOED's inventory? [15]
  • Is the site outside protected area legal uncertainty? (2024 ruling)
  • Is the capacity below the IBN threshold (200 MW / NPR 6B)?
  • Does the developer meet DOED's financial credibility standard?
Gate 2 — Technical

Can the Project Be Approved?

  • Survey license → feasibility studies → hydrological data
  • IEE or EIA depending on size and location [4]
  • Forest land clearance from Ministry of Forests
  • Grid connectivity agreement with NEA [14]
  • Generation license application to DOED or IBN [1]
Gate 3 — Commercial

Can the Project Be Financed?

  • PPA negotiation and signing with NEA [14]
  • FDI approval and NRB capital recording [5]
  • Construction financing closure with lenders
  • Community and public equity tranches (if applicable)
  • Construction → COD → tax holiday activation
Why the Three-Gate Model Matters Most registration timelines fail because developers treat all three gates as one sequential queue. Gate 1 can be confirmed in days. Gate 2 takes 3–8 years. Gate 3 can run in parallel with late-stage Gate 2 activities. The forest clearance application — the most documented bottleneck in Gate 2 — must be filed in Month 3 of the survey period, not after Gate 2 closes. This single scheduling decision is the largest controllable variable in Nepal hydropower development timelines.

III. The Survey License (Adhyayan Anumati Patra) Verify Availability First

Entity Definition — Survey License

A Survey License (Adhyayan Anumati Patra) is a preliminary permit issued by Nepal's Department of Electricity Development (DOED) granting a developer exclusive rights to conduct feasibility studies, hydrological assessments, and environmental baseline surveys on a designated river stretch for a period of up to 5 years. [1] It does not authorize construction, water diversion, or any permanent infrastructure.

Survey licenses are issued on a first-come, first-served basis from DOED's national river inventory — a register of all river stretches and their current license status. [15] Before any application preparation, developers must confirm the target stretch is unlicensed, not reserved for government projects, and not within a protected area zone made legally uncertain by the 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling.

IV. The Generation License (Utpadan Anumati Patra) Legal Confirmation Required

Entity Definition — Generation License

A Generation License (Utpadan Anumati Patra) is the operational permit issued by DOED or IBN authorizing a developer to construct and operate a hydropower plant in Nepal. [1] Under the Electricity Act 1992, licenses may be granted for up to 50 years; in practice, DOED issues 30–35-year licenses for most projects, with export-oriented projects capped at 30 years. At expiry, all assets transfer to the Government of Nepal under the BOOT model without compensation.

Electricity Act 1992 — Statutory Maximum [1]

The Act permits generation licenses of up to 50 years for all categories. Transmission and distribution licenses carry the same statutory maximum under the same Act.

DOED Practice — What Is Actually Issued

In practice: 30–35 years for most projects; 30 years for export-oriented projects. No published statutory provision explains the departure from the 50-year maximum. [8][9] This discrepancy requires legal inquiry for any specific project.

VIII. PPA with NEA: Tariff Structure, Seasonality, and Bankability Expert Level

Entity Definition — PPA and NEA

A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) is a long-term take-or-pay contract under which Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) commits to purchase electricity from an Independent Power Producer (IPP) at agreed tariff rates over the license period. [14] NEA (Nepal Electricity Authority) is the state utility, grid operator, and primary off-taker for all domestic hydropower production. No construction lender will finance a hydropower project without a signed PPA or PPA-in-principle from NEA.

Fixed ERC Tariff — Up to ~25 MW [14]

ERC-set seasonal rates: wet season ~NPR 4.80/unit (June–November), dry season ~NPR 8.40/unit (December–May), with 3–5% annual escalation for 8 years. Rates are periodically revised — confirm current rates with ERC or NEA before financial modeling.

Negotiated Tariff — Above ~25 MW [14]

Bilateral negotiation with NEA based on project IRR, capital cost, and risk allocation. No published fixed rate applies. Published IRR benchmarks of 14–18% for Nepal hydropower are illustrative targets — not actual negotiated outcomes. The tariff for any specific project is determined in the PPA negotiation.

XI. Who Should NOT Apply for a Hydropower License in Nepal Read Before Applying

This section addresses a question that no other Nepal hydropower guide answers. Knowing when not to apply avoids the most expensive version of Gate 1 failure — preparation costs with zero refund and a rejection that delays the project further than the time spent on a pre-application check would have cost.

✗

Projects Under 1 MW

Projects below 1 MW fall under a different regulatory framework — micro-hydropower provisions — that does not require a standard DOED survey or generation license. Applying under the standard framework is administratively incorrect and will result in redirection. Confirm the applicable sub-1MW regulatory pathway directly with DOED.

✗

Sites Inside or Adjacent to Protected Area Boundaries (Post-2024)

Following the 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling, applications for sites within national parks, conservation areas, or buffer zones face legal uncertainty. [8] DOED has suspended or declined to process several applications pending legal clarification. Until the ruling's scope is settled by further court interpretation or legislative amendment, these applications carry material rejection risk.

✗

River Stretches Already Licensed or Reserved

A river stretch already under survey or generation license is unavailable for new applications. DOED's first-come, first-served system means a stretch cannot have two concurrent survey licenses. Applying without confirming inventory availability wastes preparation costs with no recovery pathway. [15]

✗

Developers Who Cannot Meet DOED's Financial Credibility Standard

DOED has discretion to reject applications where the developer's financial credibility certificate is from an unrecognized institution, is outdated (generally over 6 months), or is inconsistent with the scale of the proposed project. Rejection on this ground is common for first-time applicants using certificates from lesser-known foreign banks. Confirm DOED's current acceptable institutions before preparing the application package.

✗

Projects Requiring Transboundary Water Rights

Projects on rivers subject to international treaties — including the Mahakali Treaty with India and the Koshi and Gandaki agreements — involve an additional approval layer that a standard DOED survey license does not resolve. Transboundary dimensions require Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Energy engagement before DOED application, not concurrently. [2]

✗

Investors Expecting Statutory Timelines

This is a systemic rather than regulatory disqualification. An investor who has modeled a 3–5-year development timeline and cannot absorb a 15–36-month RCOD slippage — whether through flexible financing covenants, construction-phase cost buffers, or extended pre-COD equity — is undercapitalized for Nepal's empirical development reality. [12]

XII. Common Misconceptions About Hydropower Registration in Nepal Myth vs. Reality

Myth

All hydropower projects in Nepal require Investment Board Nepal (IBN) approval.

Reality

Only projects above 200 MW capacity or NPR 6 billion in total investment require IBN jurisdiction under the PPP & Investment Act 2019. [6] Projects below both thresholds are handled by DOED for licensing and DoI for FDI approval. The majority of Nepal's 347+ privately developed projects fall within the DOED/DoI pathway.

Myth

Foreign investors cannot fully own a hydropower project in Nepal.

Reality

FITTA 2019 explicitly permits up to 100% foreign equity in hydropower generation companies. [5] Hydropower is not on FITTA's negative list. The 10% community equity and 10% IPO tranches that appear in many projects are market conventions for social license — not legal requirements for foreign-owned entities.

Myth

The 10-year tax holiday begins when the generation license is issued.

Reality

The 100% income tax exemption runs for 10 years from Commercial Operation Date (COD), not from generation license issuance. [5] A project delayed by 18 months to COD loses 18 months of tax holiday. This distinction is among the most frequently misunderstood provisions in Nepal hydropower financial modeling.

Myth

Nepal's Electricity Act permits generation licenses of up to 50 years, so most projects get 50-year licenses.

Reality

While the Electricity Act 1992 sets a 50-year statutory maximum, DOED's actual practice issues licenses for 30–35 years for domestic projects and 30 years for export-oriented projects. [1][8] The gap between the legal maximum and the operational norm is unresolved in published legislation and secondary legal analysis.

Myth

PPA tariff rates are publicly fixed and apply to all hydropower projects.

Reality

Fixed ERC tariffs — approximately NPR 4.80/unit wet, NPR 8.40/unit dry — apply only to run-of-river projects up to approximately 25 MW. [14] Larger projects negotiate tariffs bilaterally with NEA based on project-specific IRR and capital cost. No published standard tariff applies to these negotiations.

XIII. Case Studies: Arun III, West Seti, and the 25 MW Benchmark Named Projects

Arun III (900 MW) — The IBN Export Model

Developed by SJVN Limited of India on the Arun River via an IBN-negotiated PDA. Nepal receives 21.9% of generated power free of charge; remaining output exported to India under a long-term intergovernmental PPA. [11] The project required a dedicated transmission corridor built in parallel with generation construction — confirming that large export-oriented projects must plan evacuation infrastructure from the survey stage, not post-COD. BOOT provisions apply at concession expiry; all assets transfer to the Government of Nepal.

West Seti (750 MW) — The Cautionary Case

West Seti has been in various stages of development since the 1990s. At least two major international developers — Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation (Australia) and China Three Gorges Corporation — formally withdrew after years of investment in pre-development studies. Primary reasons cited: inability to reach bankable PPA terms with NEA, transmission corridor uncertainty, and reservoir displacement compensation disputes. West Seti demonstrates that technical resource potential and a signed generation license do not by themselves produce a bankable project. Gate 3 commercial viability — specifically a PPA that lenders will accept — is the constraint that has repeatedly defeated this project.

I'm a foreign investor with USD 30M ready for a 50 MW Nepal hydropower project. What's my first step?
Confirm a specific river stretch is available in DOED's current inventory — before engaging any lawyer, consultant, or study team. We have a signed generation license and completed EIA but NEA is delaying PPA signing. What are our options?
You're at Gate 3 of the Three-Gate model — technically approved, commercially stuck. NEA's PPA delays are not unique to your project: West Seti's failed development involved exactly this dynamic. Options include: escalating through IBN if your project meets the threshold; engaging the Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) on tariff confirmation to reduce NEA's internal uncertainty; or exploring export PPA frameworks if your site has grid access to cross-border lines. None of these are fast. All require active legal and commercial representation — this is the point in hydropower development where the difference between a completed project and a stranded license is professional intervention. [14]
Our project is 220 MW. Does it go to DOED or IBN?
At 220 MW, your project exceeds the 200 MW threshold and routes to IBN for a Project Development Agreement (PDA) rather than a standard DOED generation license. [6] The PDA process takes 1–3 months with committee hearings and is a negotiated instrument — not a procedural approval. IBN's involvement bundles land facilitation, inter-agency coordination, and royalty terms into one agreement. You will still need DOED's technical involvement for the water permit and river inventory, but IBN is your primary counterparty. The 200 MW/NPR 6B threshold is the operative one under the current PPP & Investment Act 2019, though some older analyses cite 500 MW — confirm current operative threshold with IBN directly.

How long does hydropower licensing take in Nepal?
Statutory timelines suggest 3–5 years from survey license to COD. An empirical study of 34 private projects (Koirala, Journal of Engineering Issues and Solutions, 2024) found actual median timelines of 5–12 years, with all projects missing RCOD by 15–36 months. The primary cause is forest land clearance, not construction failure. [12]
What does the survey license cost in Nepal?
The DOED application fee ranges from NPR 10,000 to NPR 100,000 depending on project capacity. Total pre-construction costs including feasibility, EIA, forest clearance, legal counsel, and grid study range from approximately USD 80,000 for a 5–25 MW project to over USD 2,000,000 for a 100–200 MW project, before any civil or electromechanical construction expenditure.
Who owns water rights in Nepal?
The state owns all water resources under the Water Resources Act 1992. [2] Private developers do not purchase water rights — they obtain a generation license granting the right to use water for generation during the license period. At license expiry, all rights and assets revert to the government under BOOT.
Can Nepal hydropower electricity be exported to India?
Yes. Nepal exports electricity to India during the wet season via the 400 kV Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur interconnection and other cross-border lines. [10] Export projects require a generation license and either a standard NEA PPA with export provisions or, for IBN-scale projects, a dedicated export PPA. Nepal's government targets 15,000 MW for export by 2035.
What is BOOT in Nepal hydropower?
BOOT (Build-Own-Operate-Transfer): the developer builds and operates the plant during the generation license period (30–35 years), then transfers all assets to the Government of Nepal without compensation at expiry. For projects with more than 50% foreign ownership, this transfer is unconditional. [1] Financial models must recover all equity and debt within the license period.
What is the difference between DOED and IBN in Nepal?
DOED issues survey and generation licenses for projects below NPR 6 billion or 200 MW. IBN acts as a single-window facilitator for larger projects, negotiating a Project Development Agreement (PDA) that bundles all approvals, land facilitation, and investor protections into one instrument. Both agencies may be involved for IBN-threshold projects — IBN coordinates but does not replace DOED's technical licensing function. [6]
Is EIA mandatory for all hydropower in Nepal?
No. Projects under approximately 50 MW with limited ecological sensitivity require an IEE, not a full EIA. EIA is mandatory for projects above ~50 MW, those near protected areas, or those requiring significant land acquisition. [4] The 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling has added uncertainty for sites in or adjacent to national parks and conservation areas.
What PPA tariff does NEA pay for hydropower in Nepal?
For run-of-river projects up to ~25 MW: ERC-fixed rates of approximately NPR 4.80/unit wet season and NPR 8.40/unit dry season with 3–5% annual escalation for 8 years. [14] Above ~25 MW: tariffs are bilaterally negotiated with NEA. Confirm current rates with ERC or NEA before financial modeling — rates are periodically revised.
Why are hydropower projects delayed in Nepal?
An empirical study of 34 private projects (Koirala 2024) found two primary causes: forest land clearance delays (12–24 months actual vs 6–12 months statutory) and community compensation disputes triggering land access delays. [12] These are administrative and social causes — not technical or regulatory failures — and are systematically underestimated in initial financial models.
What happens to a hydropower plant when its Nepal license expires?
Under BOOT provisions in the Electricity Act 1992, all fixed assets transfer to the Government of Nepal without compensation. [1] For projects with more than 50% foreign ownership, the transfer is unconditional. Terminal asset value is zero for equity investors. Financial models must plan for full equity and debt recovery within the license period.

100% income tax exemption for 10 years from COD; 50% reduction for years 11–15; 1% concessional customs duty on machinery; full VAT exemption on generation equipment; 12-year loss carry-forward under FITTA 2019.
The single most important detail: the holiday starts from Commercial Operation Date (COD), not from generation license issuance. [5] Given the 15-month median COD slippage observed in practice, [12] most projects lose a meaningful portion of their tax holiday to RCOD delays. COD definition must be identical in the generation license and PPA — a one-sided definition has historically been resolved in NEA's favor in disputed cases.
What environmental approval is required for hydropower in Nepal?
Projects below ~50 MW require an IEE. Projects above ~50 MW, near protected areas, or requiring significant land acquisition require a full EIA with public consultations. The 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling creates site-specific legal uncertainty for projects adjacent to national parks and conservation areas.
Forest land clearance — a separate process from the IEE/EIA — is the single most documented cause of construction delay in Nepal hydropower, with actual median timelines of 12–24 months against a statutory expectation of 6–12 months. [12] The forest clearance application must be initiated in Month 3 of the survey period, not after the generation license is issued. Sites near protected area boundaries additionally require a current written legal opinion on the 2024 ruling's effect — no general guidance, including this article, substitutes for that site-specific analysis.
What is the PPA tariff for hydropower in Nepal?
For run-of-river projects up to ~25 MW: ERC fixed rates of approximately NPR 4.80/unit (wet season) and NPR 8.40/unit (dry season) with 3–5% annual escalation for 8 years. Projects above ~25 MW negotiate bilateral tariffs with NEA.
The wet/dry tariff asymmetry reflects Nepal's monsoon hydrology — run-of-river plants generate 60–70% more power during the June–November wet season than during the dry winter months. [14] This seasonality is the central financial planning challenge for Nepal hydropower: dry-season debt service coverage ratios, not annual averages, are the critical lender constraint. ERC rates cited here are current as of June 2026 and should be confirmed with ERC or NEA before financial modeling, as schedules are revised periodically.

title: FDI Registration Process in Nepal: Complete Step-by-Step Guide (2026)
content:
Disclosure: Pluto Associates is a law firm based in Kathmandu that provides FDI advisory and registration services. This guide is general information based on the laws cited below, not legal advice for your specific project.

Quick Answer: How Does FDI Registration Work in Nepal?

Foreign direct investment in Nepal is registered through five core stages: (1) industry approval from the Department of Industry (DOI) or Investment Board Nepal (IBN), (2) company incorporation at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR), (3) tax and local business registration, (4) industry registration, and (5) capital inflow approval from Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). The full process typically takes 3–5 months, and the legal minimum investment is NPR 20 million (~USD 150,000) under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act, 2075 (FITTA).

Key Fact Detail
Governing law FITTA 2075 (2019); Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Regulations, 2077; Companies Act 2063
Minimum investment NPR 20 million per foreign investor
Approval authority Department of Industry (DOI) or Investment Board Nepal (IBN, for projects above NPR 4 billion)
Capital regulator Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB)
Typical timeline 3–5 months end-to-end
Investment routes Equity investment, loan investment, re-investment of profits

In our practice at Pluto Associates, most delays come not from the law itself but from incomplete documentation at the DOI stage and banking friction at the NRB stage — both avoidable with early preparation.

What Counts as Foreign Direct Investment in Nepal?

Under FITTA, FDI means an investment made by a foreign investor in Nepal through one of three routes:

  1. Equity investment — the foreign investor subscribes to shares of a Nepali company (wholly owned subsidiary or joint venture).
  2. Loan investment — loans or credit facilities provided by the foreign investor to the Nepali company.
  3. Re-investment — profits earned in Nepal that are reinvested into the same or another industry.

FITTA also covers technology transfer agreements (licensing, management, franchise know-how), which can be registered alongside equity investment.

Who Qualifies as a Foreign Investor?

  • Foreign citizens, foreign companies, firms, or organizations
  • Non-Resident Nepalis (NRNs) holding NRN citizenship or an NRN card under the relevant rules
  • Indian nationals and companies, who follow the same FITTA route (the India–Nepal Treaty of Transit and trade arrangements affect banking logistics, not the approval pathway)

Where FDI Is Restricted

The negative list under FITTA bars foreign investment in certain sectors — including primary agriculture, real estate (excluding construction development under specified conditions), retail business below specified thresholds, internal courier services, local catering, money changer/remittance services, travel and guide services, and others. We verify the current negative list against the latest Finance Act before any filing, because it changes year to year.

The FDI Registration Process in Nepal: 8 Steps

Based on filings our team has handled since 2019, here is the sequence we follow for a typical wholly owned subsidiary.

Step 1: Company Name Reservation and Preliminary Structuring

Before approaching the DOI, we reserve the proposed company name at the Office of the Company Registrar and finalize the shareholding structure, scope of industry, and registered address. Getting the industry classification right at this stage prevents rework later — the DOI approves your project, and the OCR registers your company, and both must match.

Timeline: 2–3 days for name clearance.

Step 2: Application for Foreign Investment Approval (DOI or IBN)

The application is filed online through the DOI's company/industry registration system (or with IBN for large projects). You must submit:

  • Project report covering background, market analysis, technical and financial aspects, funding plan, and implementation schedule
  • Bio-data and passport copies of the foreign investor/directors
  • Certificate of incorporation, memorandum, and articles of association of the investing entity (apostilled/notarized and translated if applicable)
  • Board resolution of the foreign investor authorizing the Nepal investment
  • Financial credibility certificate (bank statement or letter) from the investor's bank
  • Power of attorney appointing a Nepal-based representative
  • Joint venture agreement, if applicable
  • Commitment letter regarding profit repatriation conditions

Timeline: 1–2 weeks for screening; approval certificate issued once the DOI is satisfied the project meets FITTA criteria.

Step 3: Company Incorporation at the Office of the Company Registrar

With the FDI approval letter in hand, the company is incorporated under the Companies Act, 2063:

  • File the memorandum and articles of association (in the prescribed format)
  • Pay registration fees (calculated on authorized capital)
  • Receive the certificate of incorporation

Timeline: roughly 1 week after a complete filing.

Step 4: Tax Registration (PAN/VAT) and Local Ward Registration

The new company obtains a Permanent Account Number (PAN) — and VAT registration where turnover thresholds apply — from the Inland Revenue Department, then registers with the local ward office and obtains a recommendation letter from the local level.

Timeline: about 1 week combined.

Step 5: Industry Registration at the DOI

The company then registers the industry itself at the DOI (small, medium, or large scale depending on fixed capital). Industry registration is what unlocks later benefits such as tax incentives and repatriation facilities tied to the approved project.

Timeline: 1–2 weeks.

Step 6: Non-Blacklisting Certificate

A non-blacklisted certificate from the Credit Information Bureau confirms neither the investor nor the company carries defaulted-loan history — a standard requirement banks will ask for at the capital-injection stage.

Step 7: NRB Approval and Capital Injection

This is the step foreign investors most often underestimate. To bring investment funds into Nepal:

  1. Open a corporate bank account (a foreign currency account may be opened for the purpose of receiving capital)
  2. Apply to NRB (through the commercial bank) for approval to remit the investment
  3. Remit funds via formal banking channels with the purpose stated as share/loan investment
  4. Obtain the NRB remittance record — essential proof for future profit repatriation and sale of shares

Critical practice point: every dollar of capital must enter through banking channels with correct documentation. In our experience, investors who skip proper NRB recording face serious obstacles repatriating profits years later.

Timeline: 2–4 weeks depending on the bank.

Step 8: Post-Registration Compliance Setup

After capital injection, the company must maintain ongoing compliance: annual general meetings and OCR filings, tax returns, industry renewal where applicable, social security fund registration for employees, and sector-specific licenses (tourism, IT-enabled services, manufacturing standards, etc.).

Timeline Summary

Stage Realistic Duration
Name clearance + structuring 3–5 days
DOI/IBN FDI approval 2–6 weeks
Company incorporation 1 week
PAN/VAT + ward registration 1 week
Industry registration 1–2 weeks
NRB approval + capital injection 2–4 weeks
Total 3–5 months

Timelines assume complete documentation. Apostille/consular legalization of home-country corporate documents frequently adds 2–4 weeks if not started early.

Indicative Government Fees and Costs

Government fees depend on authorized capital and industry scale (registration fee slabs under the Companies Act and DOI schedules change with each Finance Act). Beyond government fees, budget for document apostille/notarization, certified translations, and professional fees. We provide a written fee estimate after reviewing the project structure — see our FDI service page.

Common Reasons FDI Applications Face Delay or Rejection

From files we have reviewed and remediated, the recurring issues are:

  1. Weak project report — no credible market sizing, unrealistic financials, or mismatch between declared scope and actual activity
  2. Credibility documentation gaps — bank letters that don't meet the DOI's expectations on format or recency
  3. Negative-list conflict — proposing activity that falls under the restricted list without realizing it
  4. Structure mismatches — shareholding in the MoA that doesn't match the FDI approval
  5. Banking channel errors — remitting funds before NRB recording, or through informal channels, which jeopardizes repatriation rights

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the minimum FDI amount in Nepal?

NPR 20 million per foreign investor, per FITTA 2075. This applies to equity investment; the amount must be brought in through formal banking channels.

Can a foreigner own 100% of a company in Nepal?

Yes, in most sectors. FITTA permits wholly foreign-owned companies except in sectors on the negative list or where specific laws require local participation.

How long does the FDI process take?

Realistically 3–5 months from name clearance to recorded capital injection, assuming documents are ready when filings begin.

Do Indian investors follow a different process?

No separate approval track exists — Indian investors use the same DOI/IBN route. Practical differences arise in banking documentation under India–Nepal treaty arrangements.

Can profits be repatriated out of Nepal?

Yes. FITTA guarantees repatriation of profits, dividends, and sale proceeds — provided the original investment was properly recorded with NRB. This is why Step 7 discipline matters.

Is physical presence in Nepal required?

Not for the registration stages; a power of attorney allows a Nepal-based lawyer to file on your behalf. Directors will need visit visas for banking formalities and operations in most cases.

title: How Foreign Investors Can Set Up a Company in Nepal in 2025
content:
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) has become one of the most discussed topics in Nepal's economic policy. As the government continues to liberalise the investment climate, foreign companies are exploring entry into sectors ranging from hydropower and tourism to manufacturing and information technology.

Legal framework for foreign investment

The principal legislation governing foreign investment is the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), 2075, read together with the Companies Act, 2063. FITTA establishes the framework for foreign investment approval, repatriation rights, and sectoral limits, while the Companies Act governs how a foreign-owned entity is formed and administered.

Choosing the right corporate structure

Most foreign investors incorporate either a private limited company or a public limited company under the Companies Act, 2063. The private limited structure remains the most common for wholly owned subsidiaries because it offers flexibility in governance and simpler reporting obligations.

Step-by-step incorporation process

The typical process of establishing a company in Nepal involves the following steps:

  • Name clearance from the Office of the Company Registrar
  • Drafting and notarising the memorandum and articles of association
  • Filing incorporation documents and obtaining the certificate of incorporation
  • Registering with the tax authority and obtaining a Permanent Account Number (PAN)
  • Opening a corporate bank account and, where applicable, registering for VAT

Approvals and clearances

Depending on the sector and investment size, investors may require approval from the Investment Board Nepal (IBN), the Department of Industry, or the Nepal Rastra Bank for capital inflow and repatriation. Sector regulators such as the Nepal Electricity Authority or the Nepal Rastra Bank may impose additional licensing conditions.

Key considerations for 2025

Foreign investors should plan for rising compliance expectations around beneficial ownership disclosure, anti-money-laundering rules, and sector-specific licensing. Companies incorporated with a minimum foreign shareholding often face additional audit and reporting duties, so engaging local counsel early reduces delay significantly.

title: Key Corporate Law Reforms in Nepal: What Directors Need to Know
content:
Directors of companies in Nepal operate under a steadily evolving statutory regime. Recent amendments and regulatory practice have tightened director accountability, expanded disclosure duties, and reshaped how boards manage conflicts of interest. Staying current is no longer optional.

The Companies Act, 2063 as the cornerstone

The Companies Act, 2063 remains the primary source of directors' duties. It codifies fiduciary obligations to act in good faith, avoid conflicts of interest, and exercise the care and diligence of a reasonably prudent person in the same circumstances.

Board responsibilities that receive scrutiny

Regulators increasingly focus on the following areas:

  • Timely and accurate financial reporting to shareholders and the Office of the Company Registrar
  • Proper maintenance of statutory registers and minutes of board meetings
  • Disclosure of transactions with related parties and connected persons
  • Compliance with beneficial ownership reporting under anti-money-laundering rules
  • Approval of significant asset transfers and major financing arrangements

Conflicts of interest

A director who has an interest in a transaction must disclose it and, in most cases, abstain from the relevant board resolution. Failure to do so can expose the director to personal liability and void the transaction at the instance of the company.

Insolvency and personal liability

Recent judicial trends have made directors personally accountable for trading while the company is insolvent and for preferences that prejudice creditors. Boards facing distress should seek advice before continuing operations.

Practical steps for 2026

Directors should schedule annual governance reviews, update the company's internal bylaws, and verify that statutory filings are current. External counsel can help audit board practices against emerging expectations.

title: Trademark Registration in Nepal: A Practical Guide for Businesses
content:
Brands are among the most valuable assets a business owns, yet many companies in Nepal operate without registered trademark protection. Registration grants a statutory monopoly over the mark and provides a strong basis for enforcement against counterfeiters and copycats.

Where to file

Trademarks are registered with the Department of Industry under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022. The same office administers patents, industrial designs, and trademarks, so the system operates centrally in Kathmandu.

The registration process

The application process generally involves:

  • Conducting a preliminary search to identify conflicting marks
  • Filing the application with a representation of the mark and details of the applicant
  • Examination by the Department of Industry
  • Publication and, where no opposition succeeds, registration of the mark

Distinctiveness matters

The mark must be capable of distinguishing the applicant's goods or services. Descriptive words and common surnames are frequently rejected unless they have acquired secondary meaning through use.

Duration and renewal

A registered trademark is initially valid for a period of seven years and may be renewed for successive periods. Renewal is a relatively simple filing, but missing the deadline can result in the mark being removed from the register.

Enforcing your rights

Registered proprietors can oppose conflicting applications, demand cessation of infringing use, and pursue civil remedies or criminal action. Unregistered marks depend on passing off, which is more difficult and expensive to establish.

title: Renewable Energy Projects in Nepal: Legal and Regulatory Overview
content:
Nepal's renewable energy sector, led by hydropower, continues to attract domestic and foreign investment. Understanding the licensing, environmental, and power-purchase framework is essential before committing capital to a project.

Primary legislation

The Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050 govern the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity. The Investment Board Act applies to larger projects that fall within the national priority thresholds.

Licensing requirements

Project developers must obtain:

  • A survey licence to conduct preliminary studies and feasibility assessments
  • An electricity generation licence once the survey and studies are complete
  • Approval of the environmental impact assessment (EIA) or initial environmental examination (IEE), as applicable

Power purchase agreements

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) is the principal off-taker. The terms of the power purchase agreement (PPA), including tariffs and take-or-pay obligations, are negotiated against the prevailing regulatory framework and can significantly affect bankability.

Project finance considerations

Lenders typically require a complete chain of land rights, generation and transmission licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance. Foreign investors should also confirm whether the investment requires approval from the Investment Board Nepal or sectoral regulators.

Environmental and social compliance

Hydropower and renewable projects face heightened environmental and social scrutiny. Resettlement, forest clearance, and river-flow obligations must be addressed in the EIA and monitored through the project lifecycle.

title: Employment Law in Nepal: Employee Rights and Employer Obligations
content:
The Labor Act, 2074 is the central statute governing employment relationships in Nepal. It applies to most private sector employers and prescribes minimum standards for contracts, working hours, leave, termination, and social security.

Written employment contracts

Employers must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee. The document should set out the nature of work, remuneration, working hours, and the grounds and procedure for termination.

Working hours and leave

The standard working week is limited to 48 hours, with overtime payable for additional work. Employees are entitled to annual leave, sick leave, and public holidays, together with maternity and paternity leave as prescribed by the statute.

Termination and severance

Termination must follow the procedure in the Labor Act. Employees whose services are terminated, other than for misconduct, are entitled to notice or pay in lieu, together with gratuity and leave encashment where applicable.

Social security

Registered employers must contribute to the Social Security Fund on behalf of their employees. Contributions cover medical, accident, dependency, and pension benefits, and late or non-payment attracts penalties.

Practical compliance steps

Employers should maintain proper attendance records, payroll documentation, and statutory registers, and ensure that workplace policies comply with anti-discrimination and occupational safety obligations.

title: Divorce in Nepal: Process, Cost and Timeline Explained
content:
If you are considering divorce in Nepal, the first thing to know is that there are two distinct routes: a mutual consent divorce, where both spouses agree, and a contested divorce, where one spouse does not agree or the terms cannot be settled. The route you take determines the process, the timeline and, in large part, the cost.

Divorce in Nepal is governed by Chapter 3 of the National Civil Code 2074 (Muluki Civil Code), and the procedure itself runs through the Family Court or the District Court that has jurisdiction over the respondent's locality.

Grounds for divorce in Nepal

The Civil Code allows a divorce petition to be filed on several grounds. Under Section 94, a spouse can petition when the other has committed adultery, deserted the family, subjected them to physical or mental cruelty, or when the spouses have been living apart for three or more consecutive years. Section 95 gives a wife additional grounds, including polygamy by the husband and marital rape.

How a mutual consent divorce works

A mutual consent divorce under Section 93 is the straightforward option. Both spouses file a joint petition, agree on the terms, and the court can decree the divorce after the prescribed period. In practice this is the route most couples take when the relationship has ended amicably, because it resolves faster and costs far less than a contested case. The petition should cover, where relevant, custody of children, maintenance and the division of property, so those issues are settled rather than left open.

Grounds-based and contested divorce

When only one spouse wants the divorce, the petition must state a recognised ground and the case proceeds through hearings, evidence and, frequently, attempts at reconciliation. Contested matters take longer, and the court will decide custody, maintenance and division of jointly acquired property as part of the final decree. Because the decisions here are discretionary, the evidence you prepare at the start matters a great deal.

Timeframe

  • Mutual consent divorce: commonly finalised within a few weeks to two to three months once the court accepts the petition, depending on the court's case load and whether the required cooling-off period applies in full.
  • Contested divorce: typically one to two years from filing to decree, and longer where custody or property is disputed or where the respondent cannot be located.

Documents you will normally need

  • Citizenship certificates of both spouses
  • Marriage registration certificate (or court marriage certificate)
  • Where children are involved, their birth certificates
  • Aged statements or self-declarations and evidence supporting any claim over property
  • If a spouse lives abroad, a properly authenticated power of attorney

How much a divorce costs

The court fees on a divorce plaint in a district court in Nepal are modest, usually a few hundred rupees. The larger part of the cost is professional fees, which depend on whether the matter is mutual or contested and how much negotiation and hearing time the case requires. A mutual consent file can be handled on a fixed fee; a contested case with property and custody issues is typically billed on a milestone basis. You should ask for a clear fee structure before engaging a lawyer.

Divorce when a spouse lives abroad

Nepali couples living abroad can often proceed with a mutual consent divorce through a power of attorney signed before a notary in their country of residence, attested by the Nepali embassy there, and authenticated in Nepal. This avoids requiring both spouses to travel to Kathmandu. Contested cases are harder to run remotely and usually need at least one appearance by the petitioner or a cross-examination.

What happens to custody, maintenance and property

The court determines custody in the interest of the child, looking at the child's welfare, age and the care each parent can provide. Maintenance follows the needs of the dependent spouse and children and the capacity of the person paying. Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided between the spouses; ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately. For a fuller picture of these questions, see our child custody and partition of property pages.

Practical steps to take

  1. Speak to a family lawyer before filing so the right route and grounds are chosen.
  2. Assemble the documents above, including the original marriage certificate.
  3. If the divorce is mutual, try to agree the terms on custody, maintenance and property in writing first.
  4. File the petition with the correct court and attend the required hearings.
  5. Once the decree issues, update matters such as records and, if you remarry, register the new marriage.

content:
Registering an NGO in Nepal is a process that trips up many first-time founders because there are two separate routes, and choosing the right one depends on your scope and funding. Register locally with the District Administration Office (DAO) if the organisation will work within Nepal under domestic funding, or seek approval through the Social Welfare Council (SWC) if it operates at a wider or international scale. An INGO that intends to work through local partners follows a third, more regulated path.

Two types of non-profit registration

In common usage, an NGO (non-governmental organisation) is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO and affiliated with the Social Welfare Council. An INGO (international non-governmental organisation) is a foreign non-profit that enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC, and it must work with local NGO partners rather than operate directly in the community.

Step 1: Form the founding committee

You need a group of founding members, usually five or more Nepali citizens, who will form the general assembly and elect an executive committee. The members' citizenship certificates and, in most cases, passports are required.

Step 2: Draft the constitution and documents

The NGO's constitution is the core document and should set out the organisation's name, objectives, area of operation, membership, the composition and tenure of the executive committee, how decisions are taken, and how funds are managed. Supporting documents include the minutes of the formation meeting, the election of office bearers, and the PAN application of the institution.

Step 3: Register at the District Administration Office

The complete file is submitted to the DAO of the district where the organisation will be based. The DAO reviews the constitution and documents and, once satisfied, issues the registration. This registration gives the NGO legal personality, which it needs before it can open a bank account or enter into agreements.

Step 4: Affiliate with the Social Welfare Council

Registered NGOs that intend to receive foreign funding, or that operate beyond the local level, typically register with and seek affiliation from the Social Welfare Council. Affiliation is what unlocks access to funding and formal recognition at the national level. The SWC reviews the constitution, the DAO registration, and the organisation's work plan.

Step 5: Open a bank account and obtain PAN

With the DAO registration and, where applicable, SWC affiliation in hand, the NGO can open a bank account in its own name and complete its registration with the tax office to receive a Permanent Account Number (PAN). These are prerequisites for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff.

Ongoing compliance

An NGO must file its annual reports and financial statements with the DAO and the Social Welfare Council to keep its registration and affiliation current. Falling behind on reporting is the most common reason an NGO's status lapses and funding is interrupted. Renewals and report dates vary by office, so keeping a compliance calendar from day one is worthwhile.

title: NRN Investment in Nepal: How Non-Resident Nepalis Can Invest
content:
Non-resident Nepalis (NRNs) can invest in Nepal, and many already do. The investment takes place through the same foreign investment framework that applies to other overseas investors, based on the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), with certain concessions for the diaspora. If you hold non-resident Nepali (NRN) status and are considering a venture back home, the structure you choose depends on your sector, your budget and whether you want an active business or a passive shareholding.

Can an NRN invest in Nepal?

Yes. Under FITTA and the related investment rules, non-resident Nepalis are treated as permitted foreign investors, and the investment is routed through the normal approvals: sector eligibility, foreign investment approval from the Department of Industry, and company registration with the Office of the Company Registrar. In some cases the NRN route offers a lower entry threshold than the general foreign investment minimums, so confirming the current policy before structuring the investment matters.

Types of investment available

  • New company in an eligible sector: the most common route, usually a private limited company with the NRN as shareholder.
  • Investment in an existing company: by subscribing to new shares, subject to sector limits and the company's approval.
  • Listed securities: portfolio investment in shares listed on the Nepal Stock Exchange, which follows separate rules for non-residents.
  • Branch or joint venture: where the NRN invests alongside Nepali or other partners in a joint venture company.

Minimum investment and sector eligibility

The general minimum foreign investment threshold in Nepal is currently NPR 20 million, and specific sectors carry their own limits or are restricted to Nepali citizens entirely. Sector eligibility must be verified before money is committed: energy, tourism, IT and manufacturing are broadly open, while some service and retail activities are reserved. Technology-based investments in certain cases benefit from lower or waived thresholds.

The incorporation process for NRNs

  1. Confirm sector eligibility and the applicable minimum investment for an NRN investor.
  2. Submit the foreign investment application to the Department of Industry and obtain approval.
  3. Reserve the company name and prepare the memorandum and articles of association.
  4. Incorporate with the Office of the Company Registrar and obtain the certificate.
  5. Register for PAN and, where applicable, VAT.
  6. Open a corporate bank account and route the investment through authorised banking channels.

Do you need to be present in Nepal?

Much of the process can be handled remotely. Documents such as the shareholder resolution and power of attorney can be notarised abroad and authenticated, and a local representative can complete filings on your behalf. In practice, being available for one visit at key points simplifies banking and approvals, but it is not always essential. A full walkthrough of the process is in our guide to setting up a company in Nepal.

Repatriation of profits and capital

Profits, dividends and, on winding up, capital can be repatriated subject to the approval of the Nepal Rastra Bank and the tax obligations of the company. The key to a smooth repatriation is keeping the initial investment properly documented: the funds should enter through the banking system and the equity should be reflected in the company's records. Where repatriation rules apply to non-residents, NRN investors should keep their status and documentation current. The Nepal Rastra Bank publishes the governing foreign exchange framework.

Common pitfalls

  • Committing to a sector that is closed to foreign investment.
  • Bringing funds into the country informally, which then blocks repatriation.
  • Skipping the notarisation and authentication of documents, causing delays at the OCR or the bank.
  • Confusing company registration with foreign investment approval, both of which are required.
