title: Can Foreigners Buy Property in Nepal? The Rules Explained
content:
The short answer is that foreigners generally cannot own land or property in Nepal in their own name. Land ownership is reserved by law for Nepali citizens, and there is no straightforward path to individual freehold ownership for a foreign national. That does not mean foreign-invested businesses have no options, but it does mean the structure matters far more than it does in many other countries.

The legal position on foreign land ownership

Nepal's land-related rules reserve ownership of land to Nepali citizens. A foreign individual buying land in their own name is not viable, and schemes that attempt to hold land through a local nominee carry serious legal and reputational risk. If you are a foreign national or a foreign company, the workable routes are generally leasing, corporate holding in eligible circumstances, and limited ownership of apartments under specific frameworks.

Option 1: Long-term leasing

The most common and safest route for a foreign business needing property is a registered lease. Commercial leases are widely used by foreign-invested companies for offices, restaurants, factories and hotels. The lease should be registered to be secure, and the terms, permitted use, and renewal rights should be set out precisely. Leasing gives you the use of the property for the term without the complications of ownership.

Option 2: Foreign-invested company holding property

A company incorporated in Nepal with foreign shareholders operates as a Nepali legal entity, and in eligible circumstances a foreign-invested company can acquire or hold property needed for its own business operations. This route is regulated and depends on the sector and the nature of the use, so it should be structured with advice rather than assumed. The property is held by the company, not by the foreign shareholder personally, which is an important distinction.

Option 3: Apartments and residential ownership

There are specific rules that allow foreign nationals to purchase apartments and flats in Nepal in limited situations, but the conditions are narrow and frequently misunderstood. Whether this is available to you depends on your citizenship, residency status and the particulars of the development, and confirmation should come from the current legal position before any purchase commitment.

What every buyer should verify first

Whether you are a Nepali citizen buying or a foreign-invested entity arranging a lease or a purchase, the documentation is the whole game:

  • Confirm the land record (kitta) at the land revenue office shows the correct owner.
  • Check for mortgages, loans and other encumbrances on the plot.
  • Verify the land category and any public restrictions.
  • Confirm the tax and valuation position before registration.

Our guide to land verification and property due diligence covers these checks in more detail. A clean title check carried out before you commit is the cheapest protection any property transaction can buy.

Can an NRN buy property in Nepal?

Non-resident Nepali citizens are treated differently. An NRN who remains a Nepali citizen can generally acquire property, and many NRNs purchase land or a house in Nepal for family use or as an investment. Because the distinction between citizenship and residency status decides your rights, this is one of the first points to clarify with a lawyer before you negotiate anything. See our guide to NRN investment for the wider picture.

Practical steps

  1. Establish your legal capacity to own or lease the property before negotiating.
  2. Run the title, encumbrance and land-category checks at the relevant office.
  3. Structure the transaction through a registered lease or a corporate entity, with advice.
  4. Prepare and register the deed or lease, and pay the applicable taxes and fees.
  5. Update the records so the transaction is reflected in the land office.

title: PAN and VAT Registration in Nepal: What Businesses Need to Know
content:
Every company and most businesses operating in Nepal need a Permanent Account Number (PAN), and those above the turnover threshold also need to register for Value Added Tax (VAT). Getting both right from the start is straightforward, but the details matter: a company's PAN is issued quickly at incorporation, while VAT registration and the separate registration of each branch are steps first-time founders routinely miss.

What is a PAN in Nepal?

The PAN, issued by the Inland Revenue Department (IRD), is the tax identification number for individuals and businesses in Nepal. Companies must obtain a PAN as part of the post-incorporation steps, typically within a short window of the certificate of incorporation. Salaried employees, landlords and self-employed professionals also hold personal PANs for withholding and filing purposes, so the number follows the person or entity, not the business name.

What is VAT registration?

VAT applies to businesses whose taxable turnover reaches the legal threshold, and registration happens at the Inland Revenue Office. Once registered, the business charges VAT on its sales, claims input VAT on its purchases, and files periodic returns. Businesses below the threshold can still apply for voluntary registration, which many B2B suppliers do because it lets customers claim input credit on their invoices.

Documents you will need

  • Certificate of incorporation (for companies) or registration certificate for other entities
  • Memorandum and articles of association, where applicable
  • Details of the business premises, including the address and rental or ownership documentation
  • Identification of the authorised representatives and directors
  • Bank account details of the business

Registration steps for a new company

  1. Incorporate the company with the Office of the Company Registrar.
  2. Apply for the PAN with the Inland Revenue Office soon after incorporation.
  3. Register for VAT once your turnover will cross the threshold, or apply voluntarily.
  4. Register each branch or permanent establishment separately, where applicable.
  5. Bookkeep the PAN and VAT numbers into invoices, contracts and accounts from day one.

Consequences of late registration

Operating without a PAN where one is required attracts penalties, and the same applies to VAT. Late VAT registration also means the business cannot issue valid VAT invoices for the period before registration, which complicates customer billing and input claims. Because the tax obligations of a company run from incorporation even before revenue begins, an early tax registration saves money and administrative headache later. Our guide to setting up a company in Nepal covers where these steps sit in the overall process.

Annual tax compliance after registration

With PAN and VAT in place, the ongoing obligations begin: monthly or periodic VAT returns, social security contributions if you have employees, and the annual corporate income tax return with the audited financial statements. Missing a filing date accrues fines quickly and invites scrutiny, so most businesses keep a compliance calendar from the start. Our PAN and VAT registration service and annual compliance support are designed around exactly these obligations.

title: Bail in Nepal: How to Apply and What the Court Considers
content:
If someone is arrested and remanded in Nepal, bail is the legal route to release pending the outcome of the case. Bail is not automatic, but it is the default in most situations where the offence is not serious or the accused does not present a flight risk. How quickly bail is granted depends on where the case is, how the offence is classified, and how the application is presented.

How bail works in Nepal

Bail is decided by the court handling the case. In the early stage, the question of whether to release the accused on bail is normally considered when the case comes before the court after arrest. The court weighs the nature of the offence, the strength of the evidence, the risk that the accused will flee or interfere with witnesses, and any prior record. For minor offences the accused is usually released on bail or, where no remand is warranted, on the basis of a simple recognisance.

When bail is routinely available

  • Offences classified as not serious, where the accused is unlikely to interfere with the case.
  • Where the accused has no criminal record and a fixed residence in Nepal.
  • Where the detention has crossed the legal limit without a proper extension.

When bail is harder to obtain

For serious offences, particularly crimes carrying lengthy terms of imprisonment, bail is opposed and the court will look closely at the evidence. In these cases the onus shifts to showing that the accused should be released, and the application must address the specific concerns of the court rather than repeat general submissions.

Applying for bail: what the court expects

  1. Identify the correct court and file the bail application promptly, with the specific facts of the case.
  2. Address the recognised bail factors: seriousness, evidence, flight risk and witness interference.
  3. Offer conditions that reassure the court, such as a fixed residence, regular attendance and the accused's surety.
  4. Attend the hearing on the date fixed and respond to any objection.

If bail is refused

A refusal is not the end of the road. Depending on the stage of the case, the decision can be challenged by way of review before the same court, an application to the higher court, or a writ petition. Timing matters: the review window is short, and the longer a person remains in custody the harder the case becomes to defend. A lawyer who tracks the deadlines in the file is essential here.

What the accused should do immediately

The period between arrest and the first court appearance is the most consequential part of any case. The accused should avoid making statements beyond confirming identity, should exercise the right to a lawyer, and should not agree to anything under pressure. Anything said at the police stage can resurface at trial, so the discipline exercised in the first 48 hours routinely decides the trajectory of the case. Our criminal defence page explains how representation works, and you can contact our team for urgent advice.

A word on white-collar and corporate cases

In fraud, money-laundering and regulatory cases the bail analysis is different again: these matters often turn on documentary evidence, the nature of the financial harm and the risk of absconding of a financially mobile accused. Companies facing a regulatory and criminal investigation at the same time should treat the defence as a single strategy from day one, rather than responding piecemeal. title: Company Registration in Nepal: Costs, Documents and Timeline
content:
Registering a company in Nepal is a well-defined process that takes place at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) under the Companies Act 2063. For a straightforward private limited company the paperwork is light, the government fees are modest, and the whole incorporation can be completed in days once the name is cleared. What takes longer, and costs more, is everything around it: name clearance, PAN and VAT, the corporate bank account and, for foreign investors, the separate foreign investment approval.

The different company types

  • Private limited company — the default structure for most businesses and foreign subsidiaries, with a cap on shareholders and no public offering.
  • Public limited company — for larger businesses that may raise capital from the public; heavier regulation and reporting.
  • Not-for-profit company — for non-profits, separate from the NGO route discussed elsewhere.
  • Branch or liaison office — for a foreign company entering Nepal without incorporating a local subsidiary.

The registration process step by step

  1. Name clearance. The proposed company name is submitted to the OCR for availability and clearance.
  2. Prepare documents. Draft the memorandum and articles of association, which set out the name, capital, shareholders and governance.
  3. Filing and registration. The incorporation application and documents are filed with the OCR and, once approved, the certificate of incorporation issues.
  4. Tax registration. Obtain the PAN from the Inland Revenue Office and register for VAT if the business will cross the threshold.
  5. Bank account. Open the corporate bank account and, where foreign investment is involved, remit the capital through banking channels.
  6. Sector approvals. Register with the Department of Industry where the business is an industry, and obtain any sector licences.

Costs

The government component of incorporation is modest: an application fee for name clearance, a registration fee based on the authorised capital, and a nominal PAN registration. The largest line is professional fees, which vary with the chosen capital structure, the drafting required, and the sector approvals involved, and they are agreed up-front before work starts. For a foreign company, the separate foreign investment approval adds both time and cost to the file.

Timeline

With complete documents, name clearance and registration at the OCR can be completed within a matter of days to a couple of weeks, depending on the office's workload. The full set-up, including PAN, VAT, the bank account and sector approvals, is realistically a three-to-six-week process. Foreign investments add the approval stage, which is described in our guide for foreign investors.

Documents you will need

  • Citizenship, passport or company documents of each shareholder and director
  • Proposed company name and registered office address
  • Memorandum and articles of association
  • Details of authorised and issued capital
  • Identification and PAN details of the directors and, for a foreign company, the board resolution authorising the subsidiary

What happens after incorporation

Incorporation is the beginning of compliance rather than the end. The company must maintain statutory registers, convene board and general meetings, keep share records current, and file its annual returns. The corporate secretarial work is easy to let slide in the first year, and it is precisely then that errors are most expensive to correct. Our annual compliance and corporate secretarial services keep the statutory work on a calendar so the company stays in good standing.

title: Obtaining Business Licences and Approvals in Nepal
content:
Company registration is where a business in Nepal begins, but it is rarely where compliance ends. Most worthwhile activities carry their own second layer: an operating licence, a sector permit, or an approval that gives you the standing to actually do the work. Banks, landlords, buyers and regulators all look for these documents, and a missing one can stall payments, imports or a deal at the worst moment.

Which approvals apply to you

The answer depends on what you sell and where. A restaurant needs a hygiene permit and, if it serves alcohol, a liquor licence. A manufacturer needs industry registration and environmental clearances. An importer needs an import authorisation tied to its PAN and VAT accounts. The practical approach is to map your activity against the responsible ministries and departments first, so you apply to the right authority the first time instead of learning by refusal.

title: Real Estate Licensing and Project Approvals in Nepal
content:
Land in Nepal is rarely bought or developed on title alone. Behind every deliverable project sit land-use and zoning rules, building permits, developer registrations and, for larger or commercial projects, approvals at the municipal and sometimes central level. Missing one layer early tends to surface later as a hard stop when a certificate, a sale registration or a mortgage is on the line.

The approvals that matter most

For a developer or buyer working on commercial or residential property, the priority is to verify the land can lawfully be used for the intended purpose, secure the building permit before construction, and confirm the developer is registered and the project approved before units are advertised or sold. Buyers should also complete a title and boundary verification so they know exactly what they are acquiring.

Staying ahead of the calendar

A compliance calendar that maps every approval to its due date changes the arithmetic.
